anchors.heading: Nicolaus Copernicus

image.attribution: Unknown author — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
image.caption: Nikolaus Kopernikus MOT

anchors.prose: Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish Renaissance polymath, was presented a copy of his book 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' on his deathbed on 24 May. The work had been printed in Nuremberg on 21 March, offering mathematical arguments for a heliocentric universe, denying the geocentric model. Copernicus had suffered a stroke in December; he died in Frombork at age 70.

quote.text: The book, first printed in 1543 CE in Nuremberg, Holy Roman Empire, offered an alternative model of the universe to Ptolemy's geocentric system, which had been widely accepted since ancient times.

records: On his deathbed, Nicolaus Copernicus is presented a copy of his groundbreaking book De revolutionibus orbium coelestium.
Nicolaus Copernicus – De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolution of the Heavenly Spheres)

In Nuremberg, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is printed during the illness of Nicholas Copernicus, offering mathematical arguments for the existence of the heliocentric universe, denying the geocentric model. According to legend, Copernicus, who had a stroke in December, is presented a copy of the book on his deathbed shortly before dying on May 24 in Frombork at the age of 70.
Nicolaus Copernicus, Polish Renaissance mathematician and astronomer (born 1473)
Nicolaus Copernicus (born 1473), Polish astronomer.
Nicolaus Copernicus, Polish mathematician and astronomer (b. 1473)

Nicolaus Copernicus publishes De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) in Nuremberg, offering entirely abstract mathematical arguments for the existence of the heliocentric universe. It is often cited as the beginning of the Scientific Revolution.

anchors.heading: Nice
anchors.prose: The city of Nice, under the control of the Duchy of Savoy, was captured by Ottoman and French forces under Admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa on 22 August after a 16-day siege. The Ottomans pillaged the city and took 2,500 captives to be sold into slavery. The siege was part of the Franco-Ottoman alliance during the Italian War of 1542–46.

quote.text: The Franco-Ottoman alliance or Franco-Turkish alliance was established in 1536 between Francis I, King of France and Suleiman I of the Ottoman Empire. The strategic and sometimes tactical alliance was one of the longest-lasting and most important foreign alliances of France, and was particularly influential during the Italian Wars.

records: The city of Nice is captured by the Ottomans and Barbarossa after a long bombardment. The Ottomans pillage the city and take away 2,500 captives to be sold into slavery.

The Siege of Nice by the Ottoman Empire and French forces (under the Franco-Ottoman alliance), led by Admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa, begins. At the time, the city is under the control of the Duchy of Savoy and is defended by the Savoyards, assisted by the Habsburg armies of Spain and the Holy Roman Empire. The siege lasts for 16 days.
Siege of Nice 6–22 August 1543

anchors.heading: Suleiman the Magnificent

image.attribution: Circle of Titian — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

anchors.prose: Suleiman the Magnificent, Ottoman sultan, followed up his 1541 annexation of Hungary by invading again on 23 April. Esztergom surrendered on 10 August; Székesfehérvár fell on 4 September. By 16 November, Suleiman had captured Esztergom, Székesfehérvár, Siklós and Szeged, completing a campaign to bring Hungary under Ottoman rule.

quote.text: Following defeat by the Ottoman Empire at the Battle of Mohács in 1526, the country was split into three regions for over 150 years until it was reunited under Habsburg rule by the turn of the 18th century. Despite subsequent uprisings against the Habsburgs, a compromise in 1867 formed the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy, which operated as a European major power until its collapse after World War I.

anchors.prose: In September, forces under Charles V besieged Landrecies in Picardy, but withdrew on the approach of the French army. Charles had allied with Henry VIII in February, and on 31 December they agreed to invade France by June 1544 with at least 35,000 infantry and 7,000 cavalry.

quote.text: At that time, Picardy was divided into Upper and Lower Picardy: Upper Picardy was closer to Île-de-France, while Lower Picardy, which Barthélemy the Englishman referred to as Hainaut, was closer to Flanders and Brabant. During the ancien régime, Picardy was generally defined by thirteen traditional regions, still divided into Upper and Lower Picardy: the former grouping inland areas and the latter, coastal areas.

anchors.prose: Henry VIII married Catherine Parr on 12 July, his sixth and last marriage. That month Parliament passed the Third Succession Act, restoring Mary and Elizabeth to the line of succession. Henry allied with Charles V against France in February, declared war on France in June, and signed the Treaty of Greenwich with Scotland in July, though the Scottish Parliament later repudiated it.

quote.text: She was influential in Henry's passing of the Third Succession Act in 1543 that restored his daughters Mary and Elizabeth to the line of succession to the throne. Catherine was appointed regent from July to September 1544 while Henry was on a military campaign in France; in the event that he lost his life, she was to rule as regent until Edward came of age.

The Treaty of Greenwich is signed between representatives of the Kingdoms of England and Scotland as part of a plan to eventually unify the two nations under one monarch. As part of the treaty, the two nations agree to avoid war during the reign of King Henry VIII in England or Mary, Queen of Scots in Scotland and for another year after both are gone. The second part of the Treaty provides that Mary, Queen of Scots (six months old at the time) will eventually become the wife of Crown Prince Edward (then 5 years old), son of King Henry VIII. The Scottish Parliament repudiates the treaty five months later.

links.title: De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem

anchors.prose: Andreas Vesalius published 'De humani corporis fabrica' in Basel in June, illustrated by Jan van Calcar. The work revolutionized anatomy, including an account of a successful experimental tracheotomy for artificial respiration in a dog.

quote.text: Andries van Wezel (31 December 1514 – 15 October 1564), Latinized as Andreas Vesalius (), was an anatomist and physician who wrote De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem (On the fabric of the human body in seven books), which is considered one of the most influential books on human anatomy and a major advance over the long-dominant work of Galen. Vesalius is often referred to as the founder of modern human anatomy.

records: Andreas Vesalius publishes De humani corporis fabrica (On the Fabric of the Human Body), illustrated by Jan van Calcar, in Basel, revolutionizing the science of human anatomy. He includes an account of a successful experimental tracheotomy for artificial respiration of a canine subject.

anchors.prose: Massive flooding of the Mississippi and Arkansas rivers began over 40 days while Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto and his team were passing through. The event was recorded by chronicler Inca Garcilaso de la Vega.

quote.text: The Mississippi ranks as the world's tenth-largest river by discharge flow, and the largest in North America. Native Americans have lived along the Mississippi River and its tributaries for thousands of years.

records: Massive flooding of the Mississippi River and the Arkansas River begins in southeastern North America over a 40 day period while Spanish explorer Hernando DeSoto and his team are passing through. The event is noted by the chronicler of the DeSoto Expedition, Inca Garcilaso de la Vega.

overview.prose: On his deathbed in Frombork, Nicolaus Copernicus was presented a copy of 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium', printed in Nuremberg that March. In August, Ottoman and French forces under Hayreddin Barbarossa captured Nice after a 16-day siege, pillaging the city and taking 2,500 captives. Suleiman the Magnificent completed a campaign subjugating much of Hungary, capturing Esztergom, Székesfehérvár, Siklós and Szeged. Henry VIII married Catherine Parr, allied with Charles V against France, and restored his daughters to the succession. Andreas Vesalius published 'De humani corporis fabrica' in Basel, revolutionizing anatomy. Martin Luther published 'On the Jews and Their Lies'. Records are thick on European wars, religious controversies, and scientific works.

The first large naval battle in the Atlantic Ocean, the Battle of Muros Bay, takes place off of the coast of Galicia in Spain between the French fleet and the Spanish fleet. Although France has the larger force, the Spanish Admiral Álvaro de Bazán identifies the flagship of French Admiral Jean de Clamorgan and sinks the vessel. Spain then captures the remaining 23 other ships and takes 3,000 prisoners, while France loses 3,000 dead and injured.

sections.heading: Rulers, wars and states
sections.prose: Henry VIII allied with Charles V in February, married Catherine Parr in July, declared war on France in June, and signed the Treaty of Greenwich with Scotland in July. Suleiman the Magnificent captured Esztergom in August, Székesfehérvár in September, and completed his subjugation of Hungary in November. The Ottoman-French alliance besieged Nice from 6 to 22 August, capturing and pillaging the city. Charles V besieged Landrecies in September but withdrew. Gustav Vasa crushed Dacke's Rebellion in Sweden. The Ethiopian–Adal War ended with Ethiopian-Portuguese victory on 21 February. Mary, Queen of Scots, was crowned at Stirling on 9 September. The Scottish Parliament rejected the Treaty of Greenwich in December, sparking the Rough Wooing.

sections.prose: Henry VIII gave royal assent to the Act for the Advancement of True Religion, restricting Bible reading to clerics and nobles. Martin Luther published 'On the Jews and Their Lies'. Pope Paul III issued the Index Librorum Prohibitorum. The Faculty of Theology of the University of Paris issued its first index of prohibited books.

sections.heading: Science, scholarship and exploration

links.title: De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem

sections.prose: Nicolaus Copernicus's 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' was printed in Nuremberg in March, offering mathematical arguments for heliocentrism. Andreas Vesalius published 'De humani corporis fabrica' in Basel in June, revolutionizing anatomy. Niccolò Tartaglia published the first translation of Euclid's Elements into a modern language. The first Europeans arrived in Japan, introducing firearms. Robert Recorde published 'The Grounde of Artes', an arithmetic textbook. Ralf Hogge cast the first iron cannon in England.

sections.heading: Art, music and letters
sections.prose: Clément Marot, Théodore de Bèze and Pierre Certon produced the Geneva Psalter. Martin Luther wrote 'Vom Schem Hamphoras'. Mikael Agricola published 'Abckiria', the first book in Finnish. Benvenuto Cellini sculpted the Cellini Salt Cellar. Titian painted 'Ecce Homo'. Hans Holbein the Younger painted 'Portrait of John Chambers'. Lorenzo Lotto painted 'Husband and Wife'. Lucas Horenbout painted a portrait miniature of Holbein. Pierre de Ronsard was tonsured in Le Mans.

sections.heading: Trade and movement
sections.prose: The Ottoman-French siege of Nice from 6 to 22 August resulted in the capture of the city and the taking of 2,500 captives sold into slavery. Guillaume Rouillé set up as a bookseller in Lyon.

sections.heading: Earth, weather and disease
sections.prose: Massive flooding of the Mississippi and Arkansas rivers occurred over 40 days while Hernando de Soto's expedition was passing through. The Lighthouse of Genoa was completed in its present form.

sections.heading: Elsewhere in the year
sections.prose: Regent Arran signed the Treaty of Greenwich on 1 July, but the Secret Bond was made on 24 July opposing Mary's marriage to Edward. Landrecies was besieged by Charles V but the siege was withdrawn.
